{{Legend0|#D3D3D3|No election}} }} '''United States gubernatorial elections''' were held on November 7, 2017, in two states: [[Virginia]] and [[New Jersey]]. These elections formed part of the [[2017 United States elections]]. The last regular gubernatorial elections for these two states were in [[2013 United States gubernatorial elections|2013]]. Both incumbents were term-limited, so both seats were open. Democrats held the governorship in Virginia and picked up the governorship of New Jersey. For the first time since [[2008 United States gubernatorial elections|2008]], Democrats won the total popular vote of the year's gubernatorial elections. ==Election predictions== Several sites and individuals publish predictions of competitive seats. These predictions look at factors such as the strength of the [[incumbent]] (if the incumbent is running for re-election), the strength of the candidates, and the partisan leanings of the state (reflected in part by the state's [[Cook Partisan Voting Index]] rating). The predictions assign ratings to each state, with the rating indicating the predicted advantage that a party has in winning that seat. Most election predictors use: * "tossup": no advantage * "tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean" * "lean": slight advantage * "likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage * "safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory {|class="wikitable sortable" |+ !State ![[Cook Partisan Voting Index|PVI]] ! '''Guadagno''': {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Chris Christie]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Phil Murphy]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} The '''2017 New Jersey gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2017. There were seven candidates.{{cite web | title = Official List Candidates for Governor and Lieutenant Governor For November 2017 General Election | publisher = New Jersey Department of State | url = http://www.nj.gov/state/elections/2017-results/2017-official-general-candidates-governor.pdf | access-date = September 17, 2017}} Candidates for [[Lieutenant Governor of New Jersey]] run on the [[Ticket (election)|same ticket]] and thus are elected at the same time. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Chris Christie]] was [[Term limits in the United States#Gubernatorial term limits|term-limited]] and could not run for a third consecutive term. Primary elections took place on June 6, 2017. [[Kim Guadagno]], Lieutenant Governor of New Jersey, won the Republican primary. [[Woodcliff Lake, New Jersey|Woodcliff Lake]] Mayor [[Carlos Rendo]] was her [[running mate]]. [[Phil Murphy]], banker and former [[United States Ambassador to Germany|U.S. Ambassador to Germany]], won the Democratic primary. Former [[New Jersey General Assembly|State Assembly]] Speaker [[Sheila Oliver]] was his running mate. [[Seth Kaper-Dale]] ran as the [[Green Party of New Jersey|Green Party]] candidate; his running mate was [[Lisa Durden]]. [[Pete Rohrman]] ran as the [[New Jersey Libertarian Party|Libertarian Party]] candidate; his running mate was Karrese Laguerre. Matt Riccardi ran as the [[Constitution Party (United States)|Constitution Party]] candidate. There were two other [[Independent politician|independent]] candidates [[ballot access|on the ballot]]. Murphy was declared to be the winner when polls closed at 8 pm EST based on exit polling alone. He ultimately received 56.0% of the vote, winning with a 14.1% vote lead over his opponent.{{cite news |url=https://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/11/murphy_beats_guadagno_new_jersey_governor_election_race_polls.html|title=Phil Murphy beats Kim Guadagno to succeed Christie as N.J. governor|website=Nj.com|access-date=November 8, 2017}} This was similar to the results in [[2016 United States presidential election in New Jersey|the 2016 election]] with Murphy slightly outperforming [[Hillary Clinton]] by one percentage point. However, with just 38.5% of registered voters casting ballots, this would be the lowest turnout on record for a gubernatorial election in New Jersey.{{cite web|last=Symons|first=Michael|title=NJ's governor's race cost $79 million but had lowest turnout ever|url=https://nj1015.com/njs-governors-race-cost-79-million-but-had-lowest-turnout-ever/|access-date=2021-10-24|website=New Jersey 101.5|language=en}} This was the first gubernatorial election in New Jersey since 1989, in which the Democratic candidate won Somerset County. The '''Virginia gubernatorial election of 2017''' was held on November 7, 2017. Primary elections took place on June 13, 2017. Virginia utilizes an open primary, in which registered voters are allowed to vote in either party's primary election.{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Virginia_gubernatorial_election,_2017|title=Virginia gubernatorial election, 2017|publisher=Ballotpedia.org|access-date=September 23, 2017}} The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] nominated [[Ralph Northam]] and the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] nominated [[Ed Gillespie]]. The [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian Party]] nominated Clifford Hyra by convention on May 6, 2017.{{cite web|url=https://www.lp.org/lp-nominates-cliff-hyra-virginia-governor/|title=LP nominates Cliff Hyra for Virginia governor - Libertarian Party|date=May 9, 2017|publisher=LP.org|access-date=September 23, 2017}} In the general election on November 7, 2017, Democratic nominee Ralph Northam defeated Republican nominee Ed Gillespie, winning by the largest margin for a Democrat since 1985. Northam became the 73rd governor of Virginia, and assumed office on January 13, 2018.{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/results/virginia-governor-election-gillespie-northam|title=Live Election Results and Estimates: Virginia Governor Race|first=Matthew|last=Bloch|date=November 7, 2017|newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=November 7, 2017}} The election had the highest voter turnout percentage in a Virginia gubernatorial election in twenty years with over 47% of the state's constituency casting their ballot. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of New Jersey|Governor]] | before_election = [[Chris Christie]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Phil Murphy]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsNJ}} The '''2017 New Jersey gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2017, to elect the [[governor of New Jersey]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Chris Christie]] was [[Term limits in the United States#Gubernatorial term limits|term-limited]] and ineligible to seek re-election to a third consecutive term.{{cite web | title = Official List Candidates for Governor and Lieutenant Governor For November 2017 General Election | publisher = New Jersey Department of State | url = http://www.nj.gov/state/elections/2017-results/2017-official-general-candidates-governor.pdf | access-date = September 17, 2017}} Former U.S. Ambassador to Germany, [[Phil Murphy]] and former Speaker of the Assembly [[Sheila Oliver]] won the gubernatorial election in a [[Landslide victory|landslide]], defeating incumbent Lieutenant Governor [[Kim Guadagno]] and the incumbent Mayor of [[Woodcliff Lake, New Jersey|Woodcliff Lake]] Carlos Rendo by a wide margin of 14.14%. This election was one of the first major races that took place during [[Donald Trump]]'s [[First presidency of Donald Trump|first presidency]]. Primary elections took place on June 6, 2017. [[Kim Guadagno]], the incumbent lieutenant governor of New Jersey, won the Republican primary for governor and chose [[Woodcliff Lake, New Jersey|Woodcliff Lake]] Mayor Carlos Rendo as her running mate. [[Phil Murphy]], a banker and former [[United States Ambassador to Germany|U.S. ambassador to Germany]], won the Democratic primary, and chose former [[New Jersey General Assembly|State Assembly]] Speaker [[Sheila Oliver]] as his running mate. [[Seth Kaper-Dale]] ran as the [[Green Party of New Jersey|Green Party]] candidate with [[Lisa Durden]], while Pete Rohrman ran as the [[New Jersey Libertarian Party|Libertarian Party]] candidate with Karrese Laguerre. Matt Riccardi ran as the [[Constitution Party (United States)|Constitution Party]] candidate. There were two other [[Independent politician|independent]] candidates [[ballot access|on the ballot]]. Murphy led throughout the general election, with many analysts expecting a Democratic pickup. When polls closed on Election Day, Murphy was immediately declared the winner, based on exit polling alone. Murphy received 56.0% of the vote to Guadagno's 41.9%.{{cite news |url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/11/murphy_beats_guadagno_new_jersey_governor_election_race_polls.html|title=Phil Murphy beats Kim Guadagno to succeed Christie as N.J. governor|website=Nj.com|access-date=November 8, 2017}} Murphy slightly outperformed [[Hillary Clinton]]'s [[2016 United States presidential election in New Jersey|2016 presidential run]] in the state, and won one county (Gloucester) that Clinton lost in 2016, while Guadagno did not win any county that Clinton won in 2016. With the election of [[Sheila Oliver]] as lieutenant governor, she became the first woman of color elected to statewide office in New Jersey. 38.5% of registered voters cast ballots, marking the lowest turnout on record for any gubernatorial election in New Jersey.{{cite web|last=Symons|first=Michael|title=NJ's governor's race cost $79 million but had lowest turnout ever|url=https://nj1015.com/njs-governors-race-cost-79-million-but-had-lowest-turnout-ever/|access-date=2021-10-24|website=New Jersey 101.5|language=en}} Guadagno later left the Republican Party in July 2021.{{Cite web |last=Wildstein |first=David |date=2021-07-22 |title=Kim Guadagno, Christie's Lt. Governor, leaves Republican Party |url=https://newjerseyglobe.com/governor/kim-guadagno-christies-lt-governor-leaves-the-republican-party/ |access-date=2024-03-03 |website=New Jersey Globe |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Cervenka |first=Susanne |title=Kim Guadagno says goodbye to GOP. Ongoing rift with Shaun Golden cited |url=https://www.app.com/story/news/politics/2021/07/22/kim-guadagno-leaves-gop-after-rift-monmouth-chairman-shaun-golden/8056238002/ |access-date=2024-05-15 |website=Asbury Park Press |language=en-US}} 2017 was the first New Jersey gubernatorial election since [[1989 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1989]] in which the Democratic candidate won [[Somerset County, New Jersey|Somerset County]], as well as the first since [[2005 New Jersey gubernatorial election|2005]] in which the Democratic candidate won [[Burlington County, New Jersey|Burlington County]], [[Middlesex County, New Jersey|Middlesex County]], [[Atlantic County, New Jersey|Atlantic County]], or [[Gloucester County, New Jersey|Gloucester County]]. Murphy became the first New Jersey governor since [[Brendan Byrne]] in [[1973 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1973]] to win without any prior elected experience, and the first since [[Charles Edison]] in [[1940 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1940]] to win without having held any prior public office in the state. This is the first gubernatorial election since [[1937 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1937]] in which the Democratic nominee won without winning Salem County, and the first since 1981 in which it voted for the losing candidate. ==Background== Primary elections took place on June 6, 2017.{{cite news |url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/06/polls_are_open_in_nj_primary_elections_today.html|title=Polls are open in N.J. primary elections today|date=June 2017|website=NJ.com|access-date=October 16, 2017}} New Jersey utilizes a semi-closed primary system, meaning that only registered party members may vote in primary elections. However, [[Unaffiliated (New Jersey)|unaffiliated]] voters can change their party registration and vote in either party primary on election day.{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/New_Jersey_gubernatorial_and_lieutenant_gubernatorial_election,_2017|title=New Jersey gubernatorial and lieutenant gubernatorial election, 2017 - Ballotpedia|website=Ballotpedia.org|access-date=January 13, 2017}}{{cite web|title=New Jersey Primary Elections at a Glance|url=http://lwvnj.org/images/voting/primaryelectionguide-2016.pdf|publisher=League of Women Voters of New Jersey|access-date=January 13, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116151326/http://lwvnj.org/images/voting/primaryelectionguide-2016.pdf|archive-date=January 16, 2017|url-status=dead}} The deadline to file petitions to qualify for primary elections was April 3; eleven contenders submitted petitions satisfying the requirement of 1,000 signatures.{{cite news | last = Johnson | first = Brett | title = Meet the Democrats and Republicans in this year's race to succeed Christie as N.J. governor | publisher = The Star-Ledger | date = April 4, 2017 | url = http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/04/the_democrats_and_republicans_in_this_years_race_t.html | access-date = April 20, 2017}} On April 18, as is required by the [[New Jersey Election Law Enforcement Commission]], the candidates' [[Financial disclosure of public servants|financial disclosures]], showing sources of earned income (e.g. salaries) and [[unearned income]] (e.g. investments), were made public.{{cite news | last = Brent Johnson and Samantha Marcus | title = N.J.'s governor candidates just disclosed their sources of income. Here they are. | newspaper = The Star-Ledger |date = April 18, 2017 | url = http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/04/njs_governor_candidates_just_disclosed_their_sourc.html | access-date = 19 April 2017}} Gubernatorial primary candidates utilized what is known as the "[[Matching funds#In politics|matching funds]]" program. Those who raised at least $430,000 qualified to receive two dollars in public money for every dollar raised privately. State law mandates that any primary candidates who qualify for matching funds must participate in at least two primary debates. Candidates who choose not to seek matching funds but commit to raising and spending at least $430,000 can also participate.{{cite web|url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/04/see_the_dates_for_the_nj_governor_primary_debates.html|title=See the dates for the N.J. governor primary debates|website=Nj.com|date=April 19, 2017|access-date=May 4, 2017}}{{cite web|url=http://www.elec.state.nj.us/publicinformation/gub_man_Primary2017.htm|title=New Jersey Election Law Enforcement Commission|website=Elec.state.nj.us|access-date=May 4, 2017|archive-date=April 4, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170404213415/http://www.elec.state.nj.us/publicinformation/gub_man_Primary2017.htm|url-status=dead}} As of May 8, primary candidates had received donations from ten states other than New Jersey.{{cite web|url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/05/the_10_states_contributing_the_most_to_nj_gubernat.html|title=The 10 states contributing the most to N.J. gubernatorial hopefuls|website=NJ.com|date=May 22, 2017|access-date=October 16, 2017}} The first debates were held on May 9, hosted by [[Stockton University]]. The Republicans debated first followed by the Democrats. The debates were live-streamed on Facebook, the university's website via [[Livestream]], and on [[News 12 New Jersey]]. The live stream was simulcast in Spanish.{{cite web|url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/05/how_to_watch_first_nj_governor_race_debates_tonigh.html|title=How to watch first N.J. governor race debates tonight|date=May 2017|website=NJ.com|access-date=October 16, 2017}} The second Democratic debate was held on May 11, the second Republican debate on May 18.{{cite web|url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/05/guadagno_ciattarelli_battle_in_2nd_gop_debate.html|title=GOP governor candidates argue over N.J. property taxes in final debate|date=May 2017|website=NJ.com|access-date=October 16, 2017}} They were co-hosted by PBS Member network [[NJTV]] and NJ Spotlight.{{cite web|url=http://www.njtvonline.org/news/video/new-jersey-gubernatorial-democratic-primary-debate/|title=New Jersey Gubernatorial Democratic Primary Debate - Video - NJTV News|website=NJTVOnline.org|access-date=October 16, 2017}} The Republican debates included two of the five candidates: [[Jack Ciattarelli]] and [[Kim Guadagno]], who both qualified for matching funds.{{cite web|last1=Johnson|first1=Brent|title=Battle to succeed Christie heats up tonight. Here's what you need to know|url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/05/what_you_need_to_know_about_first_nj_governor_race.html|website=NJ.com|access-date=May 9, 2017|date=May 9, 2017}} Hirsh Singh filed a lawsuit to enter the debates, claiming to have raised over $900,000 despite missing a deadline to file; his challenge was rejected by the state courts.{{cite web|last1=Johnson|first1=Brent|title=N.J. governor candidate loses fight for spot in Republican debates|url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/05/nj_governor_candidate_loses_fight_for_spot_in_deba.html|website=NJ.com|access-date=May 9, 2017|date=May 4, 2017}}{{cite web|last1=Arco|first1=Matt|title=N.J. Supreme Court rejects governor candidate's fight for spot in Republican debates|url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/05/nj_supreme_court_rejects_governor_candidates_fight.html|website=NJ.com|access-date=May 13, 2017|date=May 9, 2017}} The Democratic debates included four of the six candidates: [[Jim Johnson (New Jersey politician)|Jim Johnson]], [[John Wisniewski]] (who both qualified for matching funds), [[Phil Murphy]] (who opted out of matching funds but had spent enough to qualify), and [[Raymond Lesniak]] (who did not raise enough to qualify for matching funds but loaned his campaign enough money to qualify for the debates). ==Republican '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Virginia|Governor]] | before_election = [[Terry McAuliffe]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Ralph Northam]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Virginia}} The '''2017 Virginia gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2017, to elect the next [[governor of Virginia]]. The election was held concurrently with other elections for [[2017 Virginia elections|Virginia's statewide offices]], the [[2017 Virginia House of Delegates election|House of Delegates]], and other [[2017 United States elections|United States' offices]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Terry McAuliffe]] was [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to run for re-election, as the [[Constitution of Virginia]] prohibits its governors from serving consecutive terms. McAuliffe later unsuccessfully ran for a second non-consecutive term in the [[2021 Virginia gubernatorial election]]. Primary elections took place on June 13, 2017. Virginia utilizes an open primary, in which registered voters are allowed to vote in either party's primary election.{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Virginia_gubernatorial_election,_2017|title=Virginia gubernatorial election, 2017|publisher=Ballotpedia.org|access-date=September 23, 2017}} [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] nominated incumbent lieutenant governor [[Ralph Northam]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] nominated former RNC Chair [[Ed Gillespie]]. The [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian Party]] nominated Clifford Hyra by convention on May 6, 2017.{{cite web|url=https://www.lp.org/lp-nominates-cliff-hyra-virginia-governor/|title=LP nominates Cliff Hyra for Virginia governor - Libertarian Party|date=May 9, 2017|publisher=LP.org|access-date=September 23, 2017}} In the general election on November 7, 2017, [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Ralph Northam]] defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Ed Gillespie]] by 8.92% points — the largest gubernatorial margin for Democrats since [[1985 Virginia gubernatorial election|1985]], though this record would be broken 8 years later when [[Abigail Spanberger]] won by 15.36% points in [[2025 Virginia gubernatorial election|2025]]. The election had the highest voter turnout percentage in the state's gubernatorial history since [[1997 Virginia gubernatorial election|1997]] with 47.6% of registered voters casting their ballot.{{cite web|title=Registration/Turnout Statistics|url=https://www.elections.virginia.gov/resultsreports/registration-statistics/registrationturnout-statistics/index.html|publisher=Virginia Department of Elections|access-date=December 20, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181018023154/https://www.elections.virginia.gov/resultsreports/registration-statistics/registrationturnout-statistics/index.html|archive-date=October 18, 2018|url-status=dead}} At the time, both Northam and Gillespie set records for most votes received by a Virginia gubernatorial candidate though both records would be broken in [[2021 Virginia gubernatorial election|2021]]. [[Chesterfield County, Virginia|Chesterfield County]] voted Democratic for the first time since 1961. Northam assumed office as the [[List of governors of Virginia|73rd]] [[governor of Virginia]] on January 13, 2018.{{cite web |last=Bloch |first=Matthew |date=November 7, 2017 |title=Live Election Results and Estimates: Virginia Governor Race |url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/results/virginia-governor-election-gillespie-northam |access-date=November 7, 2017 |newspaper=The New York Times}}
